title: How do you structure your answer in a case interview?
description: The most heavily weighted skill. How to build a MECE structure for any problem, and why you must say where you would start.
hook: You structure a case answer by breaking the client's problem into three or four parts that do not overlap and together cover everything important, tailoring each part to this client, and then saying which part you would examine first and why. That last step, the hypothesis, is what turns a list into a plan. It is a skill, not a talent, and it improves quickly with practice.
body:
In this guide

  • What a structure is for
  • MECE: no overlaps, no gaps
  • Two ways to build buckets
  • Start from the client's metric
  • Make it specific to this client
  • Finish with a hypothesis
  • A worked example: one prompt, two structures
  • How to present it
  • The mistakes that weaken a structure
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

What a structure is for

A structure is your plan for solving the case, drawn as an issue tree: the question at the top, three or four big areas underneath, and the specific things you would check under each. It does two jobs. It shows the interviewer you have a plan, and it tells you what to look at next when you get lost twenty minutes in. Interviewers watch this moment closely, because it shows how you think before any data arrives.

MECE: no overlaps, no gaps

MECE stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. In plain words: your buckets should not overlap, and together they should cover everything that matters. "Revenue" and "costs" are MECE for profit, because every cause of a profit change sits in exactly one of them. "Marketing" and "customers" are not, because a loyalty scheme belongs in both. Our MECE explainer has more examples.

Two ways to build buckets

  • By factors. Split the thing into drivers that combine mathematically. Profit = revenue − costs; revenue = customers × spend per customer. Best for "why" questions, because you can measure each branch and see which one moved.
  • By steps. A sequence of questions you must answer in order. Is the market attractive? Can we win? Do the economics work? How would we enter? Best for "should we" questions, because each step can stop the analysis.

Start from the client's metric

The top of the tree should be the number the client cares about. For a retailer with falling profit, that is profit = sales − costs, with sales split into orders × average order value, and costs into cost per order and fixed costs. Every branch explains the target and can be quantified.

For a public hospital with longer waits, the same tree would be wrong. The metric is waiting time, so the branches become patient arrivals, capacity (staff, rooms, beds) and the flow of patients through each step. The right structure depends on the question, not on the industry label. See which framework fits each type of question for the core trees.

Make it specific to this client

The quickest way to weaken a structure is to make it generic. A structure that would fit any company is a framework recited from a book. Tailor each branch to the business. For a coffee chain that launched delivery, revenue is not just "volume × price". It is in-store orders × in-store ticket, plus delivery orders × delivery ticket. That one change shows you are thinking about this business, and it points straight at where the problem might be.

Finish with a hypothesis

After presenting your structure, say which branch you think holds the answer and why, then ask for data to test it:

Revenue is roughly flat, so I suspect a cost has grown. Delivery launched in this period, so I'd start with the cost of delivery orders. Do we have a cost breakdown?

This turns you from someone listing areas into someone solving the problem. A hypothesis is a guess you test, not a position you defend: if the data says otherwise, say so and move on. Avoid ending with "where would you like me to start?", which hands the thinking back to the interviewer. Our explainer on hypothesis-driven thinking goes deeper.

A worked example: one prompt, two structures

Prompt: a hotel group with mid-range hotels in major cities is considering launching a budget brand. Should it?

Generic: market, competition, customers, company, finances. These overlap (customers and market), and they could describe any company.

Tailored, by steps:

  1. Is the budget segment attractive? Size and growth of budget hotels in our cities, rivals' occupancy and room rates.
  2. Can we run budget hotels profitably? Cost to build or convert, staffing model, room rate against cost per occupied room.
  3. How much is genuinely new revenue? Guests who would trade down from our own mid-range hotels.
  4. Brand and execution risks. Damage to the main brand, management attention.

Hypothesis: branch 3 decides it, because our mid-range hotels sit in the same cities. Put a number on why. Suppose the budget brand sells 500,000 room nights a year at $90, which is $45M of revenue. If 100,000 of those nights come from guests who would otherwise have paid $150 in our mid-range hotels, the group loses 100,000 × $150 = $15M there. Net new revenue is $45M − $15M = $30M, a third less than the headline. The figures are illustrative, but the point is real: cannibalisation can turn an attractive launch into a marginal one.

How to present it

  • Take a moment. Asking for a minute or two to organise your thoughts is normal. Use it to draw the tree, not to write paragraphs.
  • Signpost. "I'd look at four areas. First... second..." Say the number of buckets before you list them.
  • Go one level deep. Name the bucket and two or three things under it. Save the detail for when you get there.
  • Keep it short. Aim for about a minute, then give your hypothesis and ask for the first piece of data.

Our explainer on presenting your structure covers the delivery in more detail.

The mistakes that weaken a structure

  1. Overlapping buckets. Test each pair: could one fact sit in both? If so, redraw.
  2. Generic labels. Replace "customers" with "business travellers and families".
  3. Too many buckets. Seven areas is a list. Three or four is a structure.
  4. No hypothesis. Always say where you would start and why.
  5. Never revisiting it. When new facts arrive, go back to the tree and say which branch they answer.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. Which pair of buckets is MECE for "why did profit fall"?

  • Marketing and customers
  • Revenue and costs
  • Competitors and pricing
Show the answer

Revenue and costs. Profit = revenue − costs, so every cause sits in exactly one of them.

2. What should you say right after presenting your structure?

  • "Where would you like me to start?"
  • Which branch you think matters most, and why
  • A summary of the prompt
Show the answer

Which branch you think matters most, and why. Stating a hypothesis shows you are solving the problem, not just organising it.

3. A "should we enter this market?" question is usually best structured by...

  • Factors (drivers)
  • Steps (a sequence of questions)
  • The 4Ps of marketing
Show the answer

Steps. Is it attractive, can we win, do the economics work, how would we enter: each step can stop the analysis.

4. Try it now: a national railway's passenger complaints have doubled in a year. Give a structure with three or four buckets and say where you would start. Two minutes, out loud if you can.

Show the answer

Buckets: (1) Volume and channel: more passengers, or a new, easier way to complain? (2) Service: punctuality, cancellations, crowding. (3) Experience: stations, staff, ticketing, information. (4) Expectations: fare rises or promises that changed. Hypothesis: "Doubling in one year suggests a sudden change, so I'd first check whether a new app made complaining easier, then look at punctuality."
